newsitem.title: UK: Uzbekistan mulls multi-currency Eurobond - banker.
newsitem.headline: Uzbekistan mulls multi-currency Eurobond - banker.

text.p: The Central Asian state of Uzbekistan is considering a multi-currency debut Eurobond of at least 8.5 years maturity, a senior banker said on Sunday.

Rustam Azimov, chairman of the National Bank for Foreign Economic Activity, said the former Soviet republic was awaiting credit ratings from agencies such as Standard & Poor's and Moody's Investors Services.
But he said during a presentation at the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) that Uzbekistan did not want short-term loans.
"If we are issuing our bond, we are thinking about at least 8.5 year bonds," he said.

Asked later in what currency the bond would be denominated, Azimov said, "I think that we could diversify. We could issue part of the bond in dollars, part in yen and part in deutschemarks but it is too premature."
Traders in London have said Uzbekistan's first bond could be similar in size and maturity to neighbouring Kazakhstan's $200 million, three-year bond launched last year.

Azimov said Uzbekistan could expect a similar or better rataing to that awarded to Russia. S&P rated BB- and Moody's awarded it Ba2. Uzbekistan's Central Asian neighbour, Kazakhstan, was rated BB- by S&P and Ba3 by Moody's.
He also said Uzbekistan was aiming for full convertibility of its sum currency.
He said the central bank had spent $3.3 billion last year in intervention to support and strengthen the currency, compared with $1.3 billion the previous year.
"I hope it will not take too much time when we reach full convertibility but before we reach full convertibility we need to restructure our economy," he said.
In 1994, the government said it planned to introduce full convertibility of the sum by the beginning of 1997.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) suspended a $185 million standby loan to Uzbekistan because of foreign exchange controls and a failure to meet inflation targets.
The government later introduced a new system for setting the official rate of the sum, which it said was more market-oriented.
